name: Nageshwar Jyotirlinga Temple, Dwarka
deity: Shiva as Nageshwara, Lord of Serpents — one of the twelve Jyotirlingas
period: A Jyotirlinga of Darukavana in the Puranic tradition; the present temple rebuilt in the late 20th century
summary: On the windswept coastal road between Dwarka and Bet Dwarka, Nageshwar honours Shiva as Lord of Serpents, the Jyotirlinga of Darukavana where, the Shiva Purana tells, he rescued his devotee Supriya.

sections.history: The Dvadasha Jyotirlinga Stotram names among the twelve Jyotirlingas "Nagesha in Darukavana," the forest of Daruka, and a long tradition places that forest on the coast of Saurashtra near Dwarka, the city of Krishna. The shrine here stands on the flat, open land between Dwarka and the harbour for Bet Dwarka, and pilgrims to the Char Dham seat of Dwarka have long made it part of their round. The present temple is a modern building, rebuilt by devotees in the late twentieth century around the ancient linga. Devotion to Nageshwara is shared across India: Aundha Nagnath in Maharashtra and Jageshwar in Uttarakhand are also revered by many as the Nageshwar Jyotirlinga, and each is honoured by its own pilgrims.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modern structure in a North Indian manner, a pale spired shrine with a pillared hall that leads to the sanctum. The linga is of the stone known as Dwarka shila, marked with small natural discs like chakras, and is honoured as the Lord of Serpents, Shiva who wears the cobra as an ornament. Outside, the grounds are dominated by a great seated image of Shiva about twenty-five metres high, visible across the level countryside long before the temple itself comes into view.
sections.legends: The Shiva Purana tells of the demon Daruka, who ruled the forest that bore his name and terrorised the people around it. He seized a devout merchant named Supriya with his companions and held them captive. Unbroken, Supriya led his fellow prisoners in chanting the name of Shiva, and the Lord appeared in their midst, destroyed the demon and freed his devotees. At their prayer he remained in that place as Nageshwara, with the goddess as Nageshwari, to protect all who call on him.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the great festival, with night-long worship and abhishekam of the linga. The month of Shravan, especially its Mondays, brings a steady stream of pilgrims, many of whom combine the visit with Dwarkadhish and Bet Dwarka. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Most pilgrims reach Nageshwar on the road from Dwarka, the giant figure of Shiva rising first over the scrubland. Inside, the hall is quiet and plain, and the linga is bathed and garlanded through the day. Many offer abhishekam here, then continue to Gopi Talav and the boat crossing to Bet Dwarka, completing a day spent between the shrines of Shiva and Krishna.

visit.timings: Open daily from early morning to evening, with a midday pause; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering.
visit.photography: Photography is generally not permitted inside the sanctum; the statue and grounds may usually be photographed. Follow posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Nageshwar is about 16 km from Dwarka in Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat, on the road towards Okha and Bet Dwarka. Dwarka has the nearest railway station; the nearest airports are Porbandar (about 100 km) and Jamnagar (about 130 km).
